title: The Day America Sank Japan's Mightiest Battleship in 5 Hours
fullText: 900 m below the surface of the Cibuan Sea, the water is black and absolute. The pressure at this depth would kill a man before he had time to understand what was happening to him. In 2015, a remotely operated vehicle descends through that darkness. Its lights illuminate almost nothing at first. Particles rising in the beam, sediment disturbed by the passing craft. Then, a shape resolved. An enormous gun barrel encrusted with 70 years of coral and rust, still pointing outward into nothing. Beyond it, the bow of a ship becomes visible, upright, intact forward of the first turret barbette, resting on the ocean floor as though it simply settled there. The scale becomes apparent slowly. This is not a small ship. This is something immense, and it has been here since 1944. In October of that year, American naval aviators attacked this ship for 5 hours in these waters. They hit it with 19 torpedoes and 17 bombs. When it finally sank, it took more than a thousand men with it. And the men who sank it, though they could not have known it at the time, came within hours of handing Japan the battle that the sinking was supposed to win. October 24th, 1944. Dawn over the same sea, warm and blue green and open in the equatorial light. Japan begins laying the keel of her answer to American industrial power on March 29th, 1938. The shipyard is Mitsubishi's facility at Nagasaki. The ship is given no public name, no public profile. What goes up on that slipway over the next 2 years is a secret, and the Japanese intend to keep it that way. They build a curtain. 400 metric tons of palm fiber rope draped over the slipway so that no passing vessel can glimpse the hole. 1,800 policemen, military police, and naval sailors ring the yard at all hours. When the ship is floated out and moved to fitting, a passenger liner is towed alongside her to block the view from the harbor. No photographs, no public records, no name on the hull. This is the Mousashi. She is launched on November 1st, 1940. Commissioned on August 5th, 1942. By every measure that naval architects know how to apply, she is the most powerful surface warship ever built. At 263 m long with a full load displacement of roughly 72,800 tons, she is half again the size of most battleships then in service. Her main battery consists of nine 46 cm guns, the largest ever fitted to a warship, mounted in three triple turrets. Each shell weighs 1,460 kg, as much as a small automobile, and can reach a target 42 km away. Her belt armor is 410 mm of hardened steel angled outward at the top to deflect plunging fire. The turret face plates are 650 mm thick, more than 2 ft of solid steel. These are specifications no Allied intelligence service fully grasps. In September 1944, Jane's fighting ships lists her displacement at 45,000 tons. The actual figure is nearly double. Allied analysts will not understand what this ship truly was until the day she dies. The doctrine she embodies is called Kanti Kessan, decisive battle. Japan cannot match American ship building output ship for ship. But if you build something no American ship can fight on equal terms. If you build the hammer that wins in a single blow, you don't need to match them. You only need to find them once. Mousashi is that hammer. She was built for one specific kind of war. A surface gunnery battle. fleet against fleet in open water. Her designers believed in that war. The officers who would serve aboard her believed it. The belief was genuine and the war made it obsolete before she could ever test it. In October 1944, that gap between design and reality becomes the story of everything that follows. She commisss in August 1942 and spends the rest of that year working up through 1943. She sorties with the fleet, searching for American surface forces that do not appear. The decisive battle does not come. She returns to Anchorage. Sorties again, finds nothing. In May 1943, the mightiest battleship on Earth is used as a funeral transport. Admiral Isuroku Yamamoto, killed when American fighters ambush his aircraft over Bugenville, is brought home aboard Mousashi. She carries his body back to Japan with ceremony. The guns built to sink American battleships are silent. She's made flagship of the combined fleet and spends months at truck, at linger, at anchorages that offer safety and depth. In I March 1944, she finally takes enemy fire, but not from another battleship. She never will. It comes from the submarine USS Tunny in the darkness off Palawan. Six torpedoes, five misses, the sixth blowing a hole 6 m wide in her bow. 3,000 tons of seaater flood in. Seven men die. She goes to Kore, receives more anti-aircraft guns, and returns at the Battle of the Philippine Sea in June 1944. She sails with the fleet while the carrier air battle unfolds around her. Her main guns are never brought to bear on an enemy surface vessel. She's been commissioned for 2 years. She has never fired her main armament at a target it was designed for. In August 1944, Rear Admiral Toshihira Inoguchi takes command. He is 48 years old. Born in Totoi, the 10th ranked graduate of his naval academy class out of 124 cadetses. He has spent his career in naval gunnery, commanding cruisers, serving as gunnery staff officer of the combined fleet, appointed twice to chief instructor at the Yokosuka Gunnery School. He is the Imperial Japanese Navy's foremost expert on what battleship guns can do. He has just been given command of the most powerful guns in human history. He is promoted to rear admiral on October 15th, 1944, 9 days before the battle. The Japanese plan for the defense of Leu is a triplepronged pinser and at its heart is a sacrifice. Laty is where General Douglas MacArthur has kept his promise. On October 20th, 1944, 420 American transports put Army divisions ashore on Philippine soil. Tokyo understands immediately what this means. If the Philippines fall, the supply lines from the resource zones of Southeast Asia are severed. Japan cannot fight without that oil. The response is called Shogo Ichi. Victory Operation One. Vice Admiral Nishimura drives up from the south through Surigo Strait. Vice Admiral Ozawa sails south from Japan with what remains of the carrier fleet. And at the center of the plan, refueled at Brunai, is Vice Admiral Tako Kurita's center force. Four battleships including Yamato and Mousashi. Six heavy cruisers, two light cruisers, 15 destroyers. The plan calls for them to pass east through San Bernardino Strait, swing south along Sam's coast, and break into Lee Gulf from the north. The invasion fleet caught between Pinsers would be destroyed. Ozawa's carriers sail south with 116 aircraft total, equal to a single American fleet carrier. They exist in this plan for one purpose only. To be seen, to draw Ho's third fleet north. To clear San Bernardino Straight of American opposition so that Mousashi and Yamato can pass through unopposed. Their crews know it. Ozawa knows it. The plan rests on one more thing. Admiral Toyota, authorizing the operation, believes he is sending his fleet against a damaged American Navy. Japanese aviators fighting over Formosa just weeks earlier have reported 11 American carriers sunk. Two battleships, multiple cruisers. Every one of those claims is false. The Americans they're about to fight are not crippled. Hy's third fleet alone commands 17 aircraft carriers, dozens of destroyer escorts, and six of the fastest battleships in the world. Japan's entire strategic calculation at Lady Gulf is built on phantom victories. Karita already suspects the plan is a mistake. He thinks sending this fleet through those straits against those odds is wasteful. Ships and lives spent for nothing. He goes anyway because there is nothing else to do. October 23rd, 1944. Before a single American aircraft appears, Karita's fleet has already been hurt. Two American submarines, Dart and Dace, are running on the surface in darkness off Palawan. When Dart's radar picks up the Japanese fleet, they move to intercept. In the early hours, the attack begins. Karita's own flagship, the heavy cruiser Aargo, takes four torpedo hits and goes to the bottom. Karita is pulled from sharkinfested water and transferred to the battleship Yamato. In the same ambush, the heavy cruiser Maya is hit and sinks almost immediately. A third cruiser, Takao, is crippled and turns for home. The destroyers go to work in the oil slit darkness, pulling men from the sea. From the Maya alone, 769 survivors come over the side. They have lost their ship. They have survived a sinking. They are transferred to Mousashi. They go below decks on the mightiest battleship in the world and Mousashi moves east into the Cibuan Sea. The contact report from the two submarines reaches Allied intelligence within hours. Japan's element of surprise central to everything is gone. The Americans know the fleet is coming and they know exactly where it is. Dawn on October 24th. Clear sky over the Cibuan Sea. Warm visibility excellent. At 0812, a hell diver on reconnaissance from the carrier Intrepid picks up Karita's force on radar. The sighting report goes back to Holly and the strike order goes out immediately. Karita sends urgent requests to the Philippine airfields for fighter cover. There are too many Japanese aircraft tied up over Laty. Nothing comes. The first wave arrives late in the morning. Curtis SB2C hell divers dropping near vertical out of clear sky and Grumman TBF Avengers coming in at wave height, skimming the water directly at the ship's broadside. Mousashi opens with everything she has. All 115 of her anti-aircraft guns fire simultaneously. The sky over the ship fills with bursting shells. Lieutenant Commander VG Lambert leads his torpedo squadron from Intrepid through it. His afteraction report is tur coming in through the most intense and accurate AA yet experienced. His crews make their runs. A war correspondent named Morris Mark is in the turret of one of the Avengers with two 16 mm movie cameras, told to buckle in tight and hold on. He is filming a kill for American audiences. The bombs and torpedoes begin landing. Then, in the first lull, Mousashi does something no warship has done before and none will do again. Her main turrets elevate. All three of them, those nine 46 cm guns built to defeat enemy battleships at maximum range. They tilt upward toward the sky. She fires Sanchicky rounds, anti-aircraft shells, each the weight of a small car, bursting in enormous clouds of shrapnel, and incendiary material above the attacking aircraft. The world's largest naval guns aimed at dive bombers. Inoguchi watches from the bridge, the finest gunnery mind in Japan, commanding a weapon of unmatched precision, and the guns are pointed at the sky. The rounds burst and scatter. Some aircraft flinch away. The attack continues, wave after wave through the afternoon. The hits accumulate. A torpedo amid ships, then another. A bomb through the upper deck. The list begins. a degree, then two, then five. Damage control crews counter flood, pumping thousands of tons of water from one side of the hull to the other to hold the ship upright. For a time, it works. For a time, by the fifth wave, Mousashi can make six knots. The fleet was making 22. She is falling behind, falling out of the column, bleeding oil across the blue green water. Kurita orders her to turn back. The destroyers Koshimo and Isizokazi close around her. The rest of the fleet moves on east. Inoguchi is wounded in his left shoulder sometime during the later attacks. He does not leave the bridge. He tries for a nearby island. The plan is to beach the ship in shallow water, keep her from sinking entirely, preserve what can be preserved. The listing hull turns slowly, the engines straining. They do not make it. The engines stop before the shoreline is close enough. The sea comes in faster than the pumps can move it out. The list reaches 20°, then 25. The order is given to stand by to abandon ship. Inoguchi calls his executive officer, Captain Kato Kenkichi, to the bridge. He transfers command. He is wounded and the ship is dying, and he has done everything there was to do. He walks back to his sea cabin. He's never seen again. At 7:30 in the evening, the list reaches 30°. At 7:36, Mousashi capsizes and goes under. She has been struck by 19 torpedoes, 17 bombs, and 18 near misses close enough to buckle hull plating. She has been attacked for 5 hours by 259 sorties launched from six American carriers. 18 American aircraft have been lost. The destroyers pull 1,376 men from the water in the darkness. More than a thousand do not come up. Among them are many of the men who came aboard from the Mer the night before. The American aviators have just sunk the largest, most heavily armored, most powerfully armed surface warship in human history. 5 hours, 18 aircraft. But there is something else in those strike reports. Something invisible until you look at the whole picture. Nearly every wave that came back armed and fueled and ready went to Mousashi. She was the spectacle. She was the target that drew the ordinance. While she burned and listed and drew attack after attack, the rest of Karita's fleet moved through the Sibuan Sea largely untouched. Yamato, her sister ship equal in armor and firepower, barely damaged. The battleships Congo, Haruna, and Nagato still battleworthy. The heavy cruisers mostly intact. Of the entire center force, only Mousashi and the cruiser Myoko were put out of the battle. And Karita now turns his fleet west, away from San Bernardino Straight, seeking seaoom and darkness while he waits for nightfall. The turn is tactical. It is temporary. 400 m east, Hollyy reads the strike reports. The super battleship has been sunk. Center force is reversing course. He is looking at the same evidence any commander would look at. A confirmed kill, a retreating fleet, a carrier force moving south to threaten the invasion. He sends his message. Central force heavily damaged according to strike reports. Am proceeding north. What Holly does not know is that Karita is waiting, not retreating, and the door to San Bernardino Strait has no one standing in front of it. At 1940 hours, Holsey orders his entire force north. Not three task groups with the battleships held back to guard the straight. Everything, all three carrier groups, all six fast battleships. The strait is left to itself. Earlier that afternoon, Holly had sent a message alerting his commanders to be ready to form the task force 34, a designated surface battle line to guard San Bernardino. It was a contingency note, not an execution order. But Admiral Concincaid, commanding the seventh fleet to the south, reads it as an order. He assumes task force 34 has been formed. He assumes it is guarding the strait. He turns his full attention to Surria, where Nishimura's southern force is already dying in an ambush. Nobody is watching San Bernardino Strait. Nobody thinks they need to be. Then the lights come on in the dead of night inside the straight. The peacetime navigation lights begin to function. The lights that guide merchant ships through in normal times, marking the channel, marking the rocks, marking the safe passage, lit in wartime darkness, American reconnaissance sees them. A report reaches Admiral Boen, one of a task group commanders. He calls Hollyy's staff directly. The lights are on in San Bernardino. Someone is threading a fleet through there. He is brushed off. He makes no further protest. Admiral Lee, the battle line commander, sends a separate message, and Ozawa's force is almost certainly a decoy with negligible striking power. That is also ignored. Far to the north, Ozawa is sailing his decoy carriers through the night, desperate to attract American attention and has been unable to for most of the critical afternoon because his radio transmitter was malfunctioning. The decoy fleet could not even reliably signal that it existed. Hollyy eventually took the bait anyway from photographic reconnaissance. Ozawa will not know until after the battle that it worked. Karita knows none of this. He doesn't know the bait has been taken. He doesn't know the straight will be empty. He turns his fleet east at 5:15 that afternoon. And through the darkness, his ships move toward the straight and the navigation lights guide them through like any peaceime convoy. And at 12:35 in the morning of October 25th, Kurita's center force clears San Bernardino straight into the Philippine Sea. The water on the other side is empty. Dawn, October 25th, 1944. Off the island of Samar, Karita's fleet emerges from darkness and finds not the massive American carrier groups he's been bracing for, but six slow escort carriers, three destroyers, and four destroyer escorts. a formation called Taffy 3 assigned to close air support of the invasion beaches carrying aircraft armed for anti-ubmarine work and shore bombardment. Against them, Kurita commands four battleships, including Yamato with her 46 cm guns, six heavy cruisers, two light cruisers, and 11 destroyers. The force that survived 5 hours of American air strikes largely intact because those strikes went to Mousashi. The escort carriers run for rain squalls. Three destroyers and four destroyer escorts charge into the Japanese battle line. Ships a fraction of the size of what they are sailing toward. Laying smoke, drawing fire, dying without stopping. Aircraft drop depth charges on heavy cruisers because it is the only ordinance they have. Kurita is exhausted. He has been awake for more than 40 hours. His flagship was sunk under him 2 days ago. He cannot confirm Hall's location. His battle reports are contradictory. At 9:20 in the morning, with Lee Gulf open ahead of him and the invasion transports an hour sailing away, he gives the order. All ships my course north. Speed 20. He turns away. He withdraws. Three days after the battle, Admiral Chester Nimttz writes a personal message to Admiral King. He writes it carefully in the controlled language of a careful man. He describes his disbelief that San Bernardino Strait was left unguarded. And then he closes with his private assessment of what separated the outcome that occurred from the outcome that almost did. That the San Bernardino detachment of the Japanese fleet, which included the Yamato and the Mousashi, did not completely destroy all of the escort carriers, and their accompanying screen is nothing short of special dispensation from the Lord Almighty. Nimitz was not a man given to dramatic language. He was a precise communicator, measured, deliberate. That is the sentence he writes in private to his superior 3 days after the battle. Not victory language, the language of a man who has looked at what almost happened and has no better way to account for the distance between those two things. The battle of Lady Gulf, taken as a whole, was the largest naval engagement in history. four distinct battles across four days and hundreds of miles of Philippine waters. When it ended, the Imperial Japanese Navy had lost 26 ships, three battleships, four carriers, a decade of accumulated naval construction gone. None of it replaceable. Just as the Philippine Sea had broken Japan's carrier air groups in June, Lee broke her surface fleet in October. The warships that remained would fight again, but as a coherent force capable of contesting American command of the sea. The JN ceased to exist. Inoguchi was postuously promoted to vice admiral. The record notes his wound, his transfer of command, his retirement to his cabin. It does not say what he was thinking. On November 3rd, 1944, 10 days after his father's death, his son Satoshi was killed in action over Tacloan, Philippines as a kamicazi pilot. He was postumously promoted to lieutenant, father and son, within 10 days of each other over the same Philippine waters. The Cibuan Sea closed over Mousashi at 7:36 on the evening of October 24th, 1944 and did not give her back for 71 years. Various expeditions tried and failed to find her. She carried no name on her hull. The JN never marked its warships that way, and the records that might have fixed the location of her sinking had been systematically destroyed by Japanese naval officers in the final days of the war. In March 2015, a research team funded by Paul Allen announced the discovery. 8 years of searching through archives across multiple countries. A research vessel, a remotely operated vehicle descending through 900 m of black water. The bow section resting upright on the ocean floor, still pointing forward, the first turret barbette encrusted with the weight of seven decades. The stern section inverted some distance away because the ship exploded underwater as she went down and the wreck is in pieces. A survivor named Nakajima heard the news. He had become after the war a chef at the American embassy in Tokyo. He heard what had been found on the floor of the sea where his ship went down. And he said he had no words but thank you. He said that Captain Inoguchi and the men who had not come up from the water that October evening must be delighted to hear this news in heaven. The Cibuan Sea looks from the surface exactly as it did on October 24th, 1944. Blue, green, warm, open in the Philippine light. A thousand men and the ship that never got the battle it was built for still down there. 900 m below this water, just below the surface of the Pacific.
fullTextVi: 900 m dưới mặt biển Cibuan, nước có màu đen và tuyệt đối. Áp lực ở độ sâu này sẽ giết chết một người đàn ông trước khi anh ta có thời gian hiểu chuyện gì đang xảy ra với anh ấy. Vào năm 2015, một phương tiện điều khiển từ xa đã đi xuyên qua bóng tối đó. Lúc đầu, đèn của nó hầu như không chiếu sáng. Các hạt bay lên trong chùm tia, trầm tích bị xáo trộn bởi tàu đi qua. Sau đó, một hình dạng được giải quyết. Nòng súng khổng lồ được nạm san hô và rỉ sét 70 năm vẫn chĩa bên ngoài thành không có gì. Ngoài nó, mũi tàu trở nên hiện rõ, thẳng đứng, nguyên vẹn về phía trước tháp pháo đầu tiên, nằm yên dưới đáy đại dương như thể nó đơn giản định cư ở đó. Quy mô trở nên rõ ràng từ từ. Đây không phải là một con tàu nhỏ. Đây là một điều gì đó to lớn và nó đã tồn tại từ năm 1944. Vào tháng 10 năm đó, phi công hải quân Mỹ đã tấn công con tàu này trong 5 giờ ở những vùng nước này. Họ đánh nó bằng 19 quả ngư lôi và 17 quả bom. Cuối cùng khi nó chìm, nó đã mang theo hơn một nghìn người. Và những người đã đánh chìm nó, dù họ không thể biết được điều đó tại thời điểm đó đã đến trong vòng vài giờ sau khi giao cho Nhật Bản trận đánh chìm lẽ ra phải thắng. Ngày 24 tháng 10 năm 1944. Bình minh trên cùng một vùng biển, ấm áp trong xanh và rộng mở ở xích đạo ánh sáng. Nhật Bản bắt đầu đưa ra câu trả lời cho sức mạnh công nghiệp Mỹ vào tháng 3 Ngày 29 tháng 1 năm 1938. Nhà máy đóng tàu là cơ sở của Mitsubishi tại Nagasaki. Con tàu không được đặt tên công khai, không có hồ sơ công khai. Điều gì sẽ xảy ra trên đường trượt đó trong 2 năm tới là một bí mật, và người Nhật có ý định giữ nguyên như vậy. Họ dựng một tấm màn. 400 tấn dây thừng sợi cọ được treo trên đường trượt để không tàu đi qua có thể nhìn thấy cái lỗ. 1.800 cảnh sát, quân cảnh và thủy thủ hải quân túc trực quanh sân mọi lúc. Khi tàu được thả nổi và lắp đặt, tàu chở khách kéo theo cô ấy để chặn tầm nhìn từ bến cảng. Không có hình ảnh, không có hồ sơ công khai, không có tên trên thân tàu. Đây là Mousashi. Nó được hạ thủy vào ngày 1 tháng 11 năm 1940. Được đưa vào hoạt động vào ngày 5 tháng 8 năm 1942. Bằng mọi biện pháp mà kiến ​​trúc sư hải quân biết áp dụng thì cô ấy là nhất tàu chiến mặt nước mạnh mẽ từng được chế tạo. Với chiều dài 263 m và lượng giãn nước đầy tải khoảng 72.800 tấn, con tàu có kích thước bằng một nửa so với hầu hết các thiết giáp hạm đang được đưa vào sử dụng. Dàn pháo chính của cô bao gồm chín khẩu pháo 46 cm, khẩu pháo lớn nhất từng được trang bị cho một tàu chiến, được gắn trên ba tháp pháo ba tầng Mỗi quả đạn nặng 1.460 kg, tương đương một chiếc ô tô nhỏ và có thể chạm tới mục tiêu cách xa 42 km. Đai giáp của cô được làm bằng thép cứng dày 410 mm hướng ra ngoài ở phía trên để làm chệch hướng ngọn lửa đang lao tới. Các tấm mặt tháp pháo dày 650 mm, rắn chắc hơn 2 ft thép. Đây là những thông số kỹ thuật mà không cơ quan tình báo Đồng minh nào có thể nắm bắt đầy đủ. Vào tháng 9 năm 1944, các tàu chiến của Jane cho biết lượng giãn nước của nó là 45.000 tấn. Con số thực tế là gần gấp đôi. Các nhà phân tích của Đồng minh sẽ không hiểu con tàu này thực sự là gì cho đến ngày nó dies. Học thuyết mà cô thể hiện được gọi là Kanti Kessan, trận chiến quyết định. Nhật Bản không thể sánh được với sản lượng tàu đóng tàu của Mỹ. Nhưng nếu bạn chế tạo thứ gì đó thì không tàu Mỹ nào có thể chiến đấu ngang bằng. Nếu bạn chế tạo chiếc búa có thể thắng chỉ trong một đòn, bạn không cần để phù hợp với họ. Bạn chỉ cần tìm thấy chúng một lần. Mousashi chính là chiếc búa đó. Cô ấy được chế tạo cho một loại chiến tranh cụ thể. Một trận đấu súng trên mặt nước. hạm đội chống lại hạm đội trong vùng nước mở. Các nhà thiết kế của cô tin vào cuộc chiến đó. Các sĩ quan phục vụ trên tàu của cô tin vào điều đó. Niềm tin đó là chân thật và chiến tranh đã khiến nó trở nên lỗi thời trước khi cô có thể kiểm tra nó. Vào tháng 10 năm 1944, khoảng cách giữa thiết kế và thực tế trở thành câu chuyện của mọi thứ theo sau. Nó đi vào hoạt động vào tháng 8 năm 1942 và dành thời gian còn lại của năm đó để làm việc đến năm 1943. Cô xuất kích cùng hạm đội, tìm kiếm lực lượng mặt nước của Mỹ không xuất hiện. Trận chiến quyết định không đến. Cô ấy trở lại Anchorage. Sắp xếp lại, không tìm thấy gì. Vào tháng 5 năm 1943, chiến hạm hùng mạnh nhất Trái đất được sử dụng làm phương tiện vận chuyển tang lễ. Đô đốc Isuroku Yamamoto, thiệt mạng khi máy bay chiến đấu Mỹ phục kích máy bay của ông trên Bugenville, được đưa về nhà trên tàu Mousashi. Cô mang thi thể của anh về Nhật Bản theo nghi lễ. Những khẩu súng được chế tạo để đánh chìm thiết giáp hạm Mỹ đã im lặng.
